Schneider's leaf-nosed bat, Hipposideros speoris, exhibits life-history traits typical of a small, tropical insectivorous mammal. Field studies of a captive colony maintained at a constant roost temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C] have provided detailed insights into its reproductive biology. Females give birth to a single pup per litter, representing the maximum reproductive output per event [N_R_i = single pup per litter, representing the maximum reproductive output per event]. This is a highly constrained litter size, consistent with the pattern observed in many hipposiderid bats where energetic demands of lactation and flight place a premium on producing a single, well-developed offspring at a time. The species' reproductive frequency is also notably low, with females capable of producing only one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year], a pace that reflects the prolonged period of maternal investment required. These combined parameters yield a comparatively modest annual reproductive rate for a mammal of this body size.

Neonatal female pups of Hipposideros speoris have a wet weight at birth documented at 2.8 grams [Wwb = 2.8 grams], a value that is relatively large for a bat of this species' adult dimensions, indicating a significant prenatal maternal investment. This substantial birth mass is presumably an adaptation to facilitate early thermoregulatory capacity and rapid early development within the demanding cave environment. This initial weight stands in marked contrast to the ultimate wet weight attained by adult females, which has been recorded at 10.9 grams [Wwi = 10.9 grams]. The nearly four-fold increase in mass from birth to adulthood represents a period of intense somatic growth, largely fueled by the mother's milk during the extended lactation period. The precise tracking of these morphological benchmarks allows for a detailed understanding of the species' growth trajectory and energetic requirements under stable thermal conditions.

Under the stable thermal regime of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], the gestation period for Hipposideros speoris has been measured at 137 days [tg = 137 days], a duration that falls within the typical range for similar-sized hipposiderid bats and reflects the substantial foetal development necessary to produce a relatively precocial neonate. This lengthy pregnancy, often reported in the literature as ranging from 135 to 140 days (135-140 days) [tg = 135-140 days], is a significant reproductive cost for the female, requiring a sustained increase in food intake to meet the energetic demands of the developing foetus at a temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. The consistency of this gestation length under lab conditions suggests a robust physiological program that is not highly sensitive to minor environmental fluctuations. This protracted intrauterine development is a key factor influencing the species' overall slow life-history pace.

Following parturition, maternal care in Hipposideros speoris involves a period of intense lactation. The time since birth at weaning for female pups is 50 days since birth [tx = 50 days since birth], all measured at the standard roost temperature at a temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This nursing phase is critical for transferring both nutrients and immune factors to the rapidly growing young, allowing it to achieve a substantial proportion of its adult mass before nutritional independence. The cessation of lactation at this point marks a significant transition for both the mother and the offspring, as the juvenile must then master the skills of aerial insectivory independently. This duration of maternal dependency is a crucial component of the species' overall reproductive strategy and investment per offspring.

The onset of first reproduction in female Schneider's leaf-nosed bats is a remarkably delayed event. The time since birth at first litter is 365 days [tp = 365 days], recorded at the standard colony temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This means a female born in one breeding season will not produce her first offspring until the following year's season, aligning parturition with periods of peak insect abundance. Furthermore, the species' maximum lifespan has been estimated at 13 years [am = 13 years] under these same stable thermal conditions at a temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This extended longevity, unusual for such a small mammal, is a classic correlate of a slow life-history strategy characterized by low reproductive output and high adult survival. This long reproductive window allows females to compensate for their low annual fecundity over a lifetime.
